## Findings by module

### cinematography-2

- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): DSLR audio is much poorer than its video, so double-system recording (separate recorder, synced in the editing system) is advised; single system means sound recorded in camera; on-camera mics are too far from the source.
- **confirmed** (ch-006.txt): Larger sensor: bigger photosites are more sensitive, have better dynamic range and less noise; same focal length gives a wider angle on a larger sensor, so matching the angle needs a longer lens and gives shallower depth of field; sensors in digital cinema cameras are about Super 35 size; DSLR sizes include APS-C, Four Thirds and full frame.
- **confirmed** (ch-009.txt): Zebra at 100 per cent marks clipping, 85-90 per cent warns earlier; histogram mountain in the middle; waveform traces a shiny forehead above 100 per cent; one stop moves a midtone about 20 per cent; about ten stops for 2012 digital video cameras; skin at 65-70 per cent is outdated, 50-55 per cent for light-skinned interviews; underexpose slightly rather than over.
- **confirmed** (ch-009.txt): Moiré on DSLRs comes from line skipping when downscaling a high-resolution sensor to HD; cure is a softer picture profile, lower sharpness, a different angle or wardrobe; true video cameras use an optical low-pass filter; moiré and poor audio are the main DSLR drawbacks. Rolling shutter skews fast pans and strobes (global shutters and CCDs avoid it); avoid whip pans.
- **confirmed** (ch-009.txt): H.264 long-GOP: GOP of I-, P- and B-frames (P about half, B about a quarter of an I-frame's data); long GOPs compress more but demand processing and make cutting inside a GOP and export slow; common fix is transcoding DSLR files to intraframe ProRes or DNxHD (larger files, more responsive editing); H.264 about twice as efficient as MPEG-2; intraframe-only AVC-Intra exists; ProRes 422 145 Mbps, HQ 220, Proxy for offline; DNxHD 36 offline; compression algorithms are not standardised, only decompression, so same-named codecs differ by camera.
- **confirmed** (ch-028.txt): Appendix E: a 40-degree horizontal angle needs 50 mm on a full-frame DSLR, 33 mm on Super 35 and 24 mm on Four Thirds; crop factors relative to full frame (Four Thirds 0.5x, Super 35 about 0.7x, a half-inch camcorder sensor 5.2x multiplier to full-frame equivalent); convert between formats by dividing sensor focal lengths with the starting sensor in the denominator. Footnote suggests Super 35 would now make a better benchmark than full frame.
- **refined** (ch-006.txt): Sensor sizes quoted as fractions of an inch (1/3 inch, 2/3 inch) are legacy diagonal figures from glass tube days, so the real sensor is smaller than the label. Shooting at higher resolution than delivery lets you zoom in 25 per cent or more in post without softening.
- **refined** (ch-009.txt): Raising ISO on these cameras rebalances latitude: higher ISO (effectively underexposing the sensor) gives more room above middle grey for highlights, lower ISO gives more below it for shadows, the reverse of film where a faster stock curtails highlights. Course line 'keep ISO low' needs this qualification; 10-bit or 12-bit and less compression also widen usable range. Internal note: handbook gives colour negative as ten stops in one place and up to sixteen in another.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Pixel count of the recorded frame (HD 1920x1080, 720p, 2K, 4K, Quad HD 3840x2160) is not the same as sensor photosite count or sensor physical size; several photosites are combined into one recorded pixel. A compact camera and a DSLR can both record Full HD from very different sensors.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Colour subsampling: 4:4:4 RGB uncompressed, 4:2:2 halves colour detail, 4:2:0 and 4:1:1 keep a quarter; gamut is unchanged, but fine colour detail suffers and green-screen keying gets harder. DV is about 5:1 at 36 Mbps against 172 Mbps uncompressed SD; HDV about 40:1; H.264 used in most DSLRs; visually lossless codecs include ProRes 422 HQ and DNxHD 220.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): RAW and log from digital cinema cameras are flat digital negatives, not for direct viewing; 4:4:4 log maps 10-bit values to a curve nearer the eye's response; some cameras handle fourteen stops. 1080p has only about 6 per cent fewer pixels than 2K cinema. Common DSLR modes 1080 at 30/25/24p and 720 at 60/50p; H.264 long-GOP versus intraframe versions; many editors transcode DSLR files to a less compressed codec before cutting.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Shoot fairly neutral rather than baking in an extreme look, because colour is better controlled in post; picture profiles adjust gamma and knee; wide dynamic range matters as much as resolution; blown highlights are a giveaway of video; bleached highlights; lower frame rate and interlace need less light; gain adds noise.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Camera choice factors: format is a recipe of codec, data rate, frame size, rate and scan; spend on glass rather than the body; small cameras draw less attention but are tiring to hold at the eye and sprout rigs; tape cheap and archival, tapeless robust and quick to check; external recorders (Atomos Ninja) bypass the camera codec for 10-bit ProRes; flash cards not trusted for long-term storage; plan workflow by talking to the lab and post house first.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Data management: copy cards to a verified backup and inspect before wiping; 'three by two by two' rule (three copies on at least two technologies in two places); hard drives fail so spin up yearly and migrate; LTO tape is archival; DVD dyes fade; flash is not trusted for the shelf; logging clips is still time-consuming; dual recording to tape and drive.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Sound often matters more than picture: a poorly lit scene with clean dialogue is watchable while a pretty scene with unintelligible sound irritates; get the mic close (boom or wireless lapel); camcorders typically record 48 kHz 16-bit; DSLR preamps are cheap, so record double system and keep camera audio as a sync guide; music needs both publisher and record-company licences, even 'Happy Birthday'.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Viewfinder caveats: it shows the camera output, not the recording; LCDs plug up shadows; set brightness, contrast and colour first; peaking at a medium level; diopter focus is for your eye only; turn off data overlays; autoexposure fluctuates, reads the centre and silhouettes backlit subjects, so use it to set and then lock the iris; avoid detented irises.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Auto white balance lags after changes, is confused by fluorescent or mercury vapour and shifts skin tone between angles; presets can be a creative choice (candlelight stays warm); skin tone looks better slightly warm; balance on pale blue card to warm; 81B or 812 filters go on after the balance; black balance on professional cameras; passive autofocus fails in low contrast, active cannot see through glass; keep focus manual.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Media handling: card speed must exceed the format data rate; format cards in the camera that will use them; label cards and reels; copy whole card structure unchanged, checksum-verified copy, compare folder sizes, back up to a second drive immediately; SSD replaced HDD for field recording; Sony Professional Disc claims 50-year life.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Power: battery runtime = watt-hours divided by watts (52 Wh at 26 W is about two hours); cold batteries deliver less, keep them warm; never charge cold or hot; DSLRs drain fast, use a grip; run lights from a separate battery; some DSLRs and cinema cameras overheat, so carry a spare body; warm a cold camera in a sealed bag to avoid condensation; check the tally and record indicator.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Gain and ISO do not make the sensor more sensitive, they amplify the signal after it, so noise rises with the picture and clipped highlights stay clipped; lowering ISO below the native value can cost highlight range (Canon C300 native ISO 850); ISO ratings for digital are system-wide, via Recommended Exposure Index or Standard Output Specification, and are not comparable across cameras until verified.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Bayer filter: 50 per cent green, 25 per cent each red and blue; single-chip cameras take PL-mount film lenses, three-chip needs prism lenses; keep sensors capped and dust-free; large-sensor cameras should have detail turned off; detail does not add resolution; chroma and gamma affect look; prerecord cache stores five to ten seconds.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Dynamic range comparison: eye about 24 stops including pupil adjustment; colour negative about ten stops (1,000:1) plus curve toes; analog video about five stops (40:1); Alexa and F65 claim 14; RED Epic HDRx 18. Sensor response is linear, with a white clip near 109 per cent (super white above 100 per cent); a knee point extends highlights. Range depends on the whole chain: sensor, recording format, display.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Gamma: film negative gamma about 0.55, print about 3.8 to 4, product about 2, so cinema contrast is twice nature (dark rooms need it); video gamma is a legacy correction for CRTs aiming at 1:1; adjusting gamma in camera works on the full signal before compression, so it is better than heavy post changes on compressed files; high gamma crisp and saturated, low gamma flat with more highlight detail. Light meters rarely set exposure on video cameras because no single sensitivity exists.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Gamma and highlight tools: Rec. 709 (HD) and 601 (SD) give a bright, saturated, limited-range look; a knee point (80-85 per cent, not below 80) compresses highlights with knee aperture and saturation controls; automatic knee (DCC, DRS); cine gammas come as display types (CineGamma, CinemaTone) and intermediate flat types (FILM-REC); DCI P3 widens gamut. Highlights lost at capture cannot be invented in post.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Log is a super gamma: logarithmic mapping gives more samples to the darks the eye distinguishes best, since digital capture is linear and spends equal bits on highlights; log flat and milky, needs viewing LUTs (non-destructive) and heavy grading, do not underexpose log; S-Log, Log C, Panalog convert by LUT; RAW is not video, needs debayering and every adjustment in post; the F65 gives each 4K pixel a true RGB sample; with log or RAW a light meter works again at the camera's ISO.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Black level: reference black is 0 per cent in digital video (zero setup); elevated blacks look milky and reduce apparent sharpness; black stretch lifts shadows from noise; store looks as scene files or picture profiles (five to eight slots) and shoot tests on a good monitor before the shoot; shadow detail kept at capture can still be crushed in post.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Photosite-as-bucket model: sampling in space (pixels) and time (shutter); quantizing error and bit depth (8-bit gives 256 values per channel, 3-bit shows banding or posterisation); an overflowing bucket is a clipped highlight and too few photons vanish in noise; more bits protect colour correction and effects; bit depth also raises effective resolution.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Compression: lossless against lossy, intraframe (DCT in 8x8 blocks, wavelet such as JPEG 2000 adopted for cinema because failures go soft not blocky) against interframe; DV about 5:1 with mosquito noise; codecs may be hardware or software; DSLR H.264 long-GOP is interframe.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Audio basics for the DSLR sound plan: sample at least twice the highest frequency (Nyquist), so 44.1 kHz for CD and 48 kHz for video; 16-bit gives 65,536 levels, 24-bit helps post processing; record uncompressed linear PCM in Broadcast Wave (BWF, mono per channel or polyphonic) with timecode metadata; data rate = bit depth x sample rate; digital dynamic range 90-120 dB against about 70 dB for analog tape; voice 100 Hz to 8 kHz; ear is most sensitive at 2-4 kHz at low volume; talk to post about the file format.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): DSLR audio kit: external preamp with XLR and phantom power (+48 V, not for dynamics), disable AGC, line level preferred (professional +4 dBu, consumer -10 dBV, so pro-to-consumer needs a pad), balanced XLR or TRS cables resist hum, wind needs foam or Softie/zeppelin, directional mics have a rear lobe and do not magnify, lavs at the sternum, boom close to the source, wireless: matched frequency, fresh batteries, show the subject the mute; handling noise ruins takes (shock mount); DSLR has bad mics, preamps and handling noise.
- **extended** (ch-016.txt): Sound levels: digital meters read dBFS where 0 is clipping; professional practice averages dialogue about -20 dBFS with peaks to about -10 (10 dB headroom), prosumer sometimes -12 average; a spare channel 6 dB lower guards against overs; peak meters show transients, VU shows average; never fix low level by boosting a noisy recorder, get the mic closer (sound pressure halves when distance doubles); record 20 s of room tone at every location; keep background consistent (turn off fridge, music); live rooms need blankets; AGC pumps up fridge noise; limiters protect peaks.
- **extended** (ch-016.txt): Double system: record scratch audio in the camera too; sync with clapper, timecode slate (digislate), or jam-synced timecode; phase cancellation avoided by keeping mics three times farther apart than their distances to the source; stereo X-Y or M-S, dialogue recorded mono; bass roll-off only as needed (filtered bass cannot be restored); narration in a booth; effects from libraries.
- **extended** (ch-016.txt): Syncing without slates: waveform-matching software (PluralEyes) syncs camera scratch audio to the recorder; matching timecode between camera and recorder allows automatic sync; jam-sync from one master clock and rejam every few hours; audio timecode rate must match or be compatible (23.976, 25, 29.97, 30 ND for film in the US) and does not set audio speed; record nondrop unless told; cross jamming; headroom against safety margin definitions.
- **extended** (ch-025.txt): Monitor setup from SMPTE HD colour bars: warm up 15 minutes, white point 6500 K (D65), set black with PLUGE so the -2 and 0 per cent stripes merge, set white where the 100 per cent square stops responding, set chroma with blue-only mode, sharpness at zero; gamma 2.2 for computers and sRGB, 2.4 for Rec. 709, 2.6 D-Cine; dim ambient light; digital HD monitors need no hue control. Brightness control really sets black level.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): (carried from the earlier review) Moire, H.264 long-GOP load, card write speed, zebra levels, waveform advantage, not exposing every face to one number, crop factor, windowing, scratch audio.

### cinematography-1

- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): 29.97 and 23.976 are 0.1 per cent below the round numbers (NTSC colour introduced 1953); PAL 25 fps is exact; 24 fps film and digital cinema cameras are exactly 24; be precise when naming frame rates.
- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): Default video shutter is about half the frame rate; safe start 1/50 s for 24p, 25p or 50i, 1/50 or 1/60 for 30p, 1/60 for 60i and 60p; gain at 0 dB and ISO low unless light is short; slightly under rather than over for digital.
- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): ND 0.6 is two stops (1/4), 1.2 is four stops (1/16), 1.8 is six stops (1/64); 6 dB gain equals one stop and doubling ISO; 180-degree shutter at 25 fps is 1/50 s; an orange 5600 K filter costs almost half the light.
- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): Overcranking gives continuous slow motion while slowing normal footage repeats frames and exaggerates blur; interpolation tools (Twixtor) work better with a fast shutter; undercranking 12 fps gains one stop but speeds motion; silent comedy speed 16-20 fps projected at 24; time-lapse arithmetic (10 s x 24 fps = 240 frames, two frames a minute over a two-hour sunset); judder rule five to seven seconds across the screen, worse at high contrast and on larger or brighter screens; wagon-wheel effect; bigger slow-motion rates need more light (250 fps stretches one second to more than ten at 24p).
- **refined** (ch-008.txt): (carried from the hand-written review of 19/10/2026) Mains flicker rule was loose; replaced with the handbook's rules: frame rate divisible into twice the AC frequency, 172.8 degrees at 24 fps on 50 Hz, 144 degrees on 60 Hz, fluorescents no faster than 1/60 or 1/50 s.
- **contradicted** (ch-008.txt): (carried from the earlier review) The course's 'bright day f/11 at 1/50 s' example was not supported: f/11 at ISO 100 and 1/50 s is too much light for full sun by the sunny rule. Wording changed to a hazy scene; the sunny rule is ours, not the handbook's.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Persistence of vision is called a weak explanation of film motion: afterimages follow the eye. Beta movement is the better-supported illusion, and a realistic image needs both smooth motion and steady illumination; too slow a rate gives jerky motion and flicker.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Silent cameras were hand-cranked near 16 fps; 24 fps standardised for sound in the late 1920s; projectors flash each frame two or three times (48 to 72 flashes a second) so light looks steady; 1/48 s exposure per frame at 24 fps gives the accepted film motion blur.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Choosing a base frame rate: 24p is film-like, long exposure good in low light but prone to judder (helped by throwing the background out of focus, tracking with the subject, panning slowly); 25p suits former PAL; 30p neutral; 50i/60i look like TV; 48p/50p/60p give smoother motion, less blur and slow motion; Hobbit shot 48p 3D. A 24p master converts easily to 25p, 50i and 60i. Shoot tests.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): High shutter speeds (1/500 s or faster) give crisp frames for stills and pixel-estimation slow motion but choppy motion (Kaminski's Saving Private Ryan); slow shutters smear and trail highlights; lock AE from changing shutter on a DSLR; shutter angle is another way to state speed; screens need Clear Scan or Synchro Scan to avoid roll bars.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Shooting screens: flat panels shoot fine; CRTs show a bar unless shutter matches (25 fps with 180 degrees in PAL, 144 degrees at 24 fps = 1/60 s, or 23.976 fps); film exposure from a reflected reading of a 6500 K monitor; defocus slightly to avoid moiré; green-screen over a monitor. Stabilisation: optical versus electronic versus software; Steadicam first seen in Bound for Glory (1976), Russian Ark's 96-minute take; lean on supports, Steadybag; zoom wider when follow focus fails.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt): (carried from the earlier review) Each 0.1 of ND density is a third of a stop; densities add and filter factors multiply; variable ND; DSLR starting shutter speeds; undercranking; camera against post slow motion; time-lapse arithmetic.
- **note** (ch-005.txt): Footnote 8 says the NTSC slowdown is .01 per cent where the main text says 0.1 per cent; 0.1 per cent is right (30 to 29.97). Footnote 5: interlaced fields give about 70 per cent of progressive resolution, not half.

### cinematography-7

- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): NTSC and PAL properly name analog standards; digital frames of 720x480 and 720x576 keep the same on-screen shape using different-shaped pixels; 24 fps is the film rate; progressive scanning captures a whole frame at one instant like a film camera.
- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): Interlace records odd then even field, two fields per frame; edge tear (combing), stair-step aliasing and twitter; deinterlacing blends fields or drops one; shooting progressive is recommended since progressive converts to interlace easily but not the reverse.
- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): Betacam 1982 half-inch analog component, SP 1986; Digital Betacam 4:2:2 with 2:1 lossless at about 90 Mbps; Video8 matched VHS quality, Hi8 added resolution, Digital8 played Hi8 and recorded DV; U-matic used for dailies and offline.
- **confirmed** (ch-006.txt): 24p recorded natively, by PsF (two fields from one frame) or inside 60i by 2:3 pulldown (four frames to five); native and PsF fit 20 per cent more on tape or drive than pulldown; digital 24 means 23.976 in NTSC territories; reversible pulldown recovers 24p.
- **confirmed** (ch-016.txt): Film at 24 fps is slowed 0.1 per cent to 23.976 in NTSC telecine, so field audio must be pulled down 0.1 per cent (by the transfer house, in the NLE, or by recording at 48.048 kHz stamped 48 kHz, the 'F' setting); not needed if edited at true 24; music playback for lip sync can be sped up 0.1 per cent on set or the camera run at 23.976; shoot video at 23.976, 29.97 or 25 to avoid speed changes.
- **confirmed** (ch-019.txt): 2:3 pulldown records every four film frames as five video frames (A and C two fields, B and D three), so speed does not change; reverse telecine restores 24p; PAL material at 25 fps can be slowed 4 per cent to match a 24 fps timeline; a 90-minute film sped to 30 fps would run 72 minutes; film for TV in PAL countries is shot at 25.
- **confirmed** (ch-023.txt): Three film-to-digital scenarios (transfer once and finish digital; transfer twice via digital intermediate with a shot log and pull list; transfer twice and finish on film with a cut list), telecine against scanner (2K 2048x1556 about 12 MB a frame, 4K 4096x3112 about 50 MB, four times the data and at least double the cost; 1920x1080 HD virtually matches 2K for TV; 2K more than adequate for Super 16), film chain and slop transfers for 8mm, 24@25 at +4.1 per cent with half-tone pitch rise, 24+1 PAL+1 adds an extra field every 12 frames, 23.976 slowdown and audio sync need, agree the route with lab, editor and sound before shooting.
- **confirmed** (ch-023.txt): One-light, best-light, timed and flat transfers (flat uses a 10-bit log characteristic and a later LUT); wet gate and ultrasonic cleaning can weaken splices; telecine weave and pin registration; speeding a feature 3 per cent saves three and a half minutes; three fixes for the 0.1 per cent audio slowdown (48.048 kHz, 99.9 per cent clip speed, picture up to true 24); crystal-sync cameras can run 23.976 or 29.97 to avoid pulldown; 30 fps audio timecode slows to 29.97.
- **refined** (ch-019.txt): Pulldown cadences: normal 2:3:2:3 (A and C two fields, B and D three), advanced 2:3:3:2 (clean reverse by dropping the third frame, 20 per cent less data) and 24p over 60p for 720p cameras (frames repeated two and three times); the A frame (only frame on exactly one video frame) marks the pattern start for reverse telecine; pseudo-24 modes (Cineframe 24, 24F) are not true 24p; 24-frame timecode differs from 30-frame timecode, so matchback from a 30 fps offline can cause cutting discrepancies; 'pulling down' audio by 0.1 per cent is a different thing from pulldown of picture.
- **refined** (ch-023.txt): (carried from the earlier review) The Super 8 scan estimate used a 16:9 crop; the handbook's 2K frame (2048 x 1556, about 12 MB) gives about 43 GB a cartridge.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Format naming convention: frame height, p or i, then frame rate for progressive but field rate for interlace (1080p/24, 576i/50, 480i/60). Composite video mixes luma, chroma and sync into one signal and loses quality; component keeps them separate.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): HDV 1440x1080 MPEG-2 at 25 Mbps 4:2:0; AVCHD about twice as efficient as MPEG-2; AVC-Intra intraframe 10-bit; DV25 5:1 with 4:1:1 (PAL 4:2:0); HDCAM 3:1:1; ingest, capture and digitise are different words for file, digital tape and analog tape into an editor.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Offline/online workflow: cut cheaply on proxies (ProRes, DNxHD) then conform high-resolution originals online; an edit decision list carries the shot list between systems; sound is recorded double system for film, with crystal sync at 24 fps, and synced up in dailies or the editor; MOS means shot without sound.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Traditional film route: workprint, mag film, edge code, negative matching, answer print, release print; grading was by a timer setting printer lights for red, green and blue; opticals made dissolves. Finishing routes: HD only, film-out, digital intermediate from a 2K or 4K scan, or cut negative.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Digital tape care: helical scan (ten diagonal tracks a frame in DV), dropouts show as checkerboard hits, head-clean only when needed, never mix metal-particle and metal-evaporated tape, roll five seconds of preroll, record lock and label tapes, store upright at 15-25 C, transfer archive masters every few years; bars and tone matter little for digital but help analog monitors.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Component video codes: legal black is code 16 and white 235 in 8-bit component (Y'CbCr), whereas RGB runs 0 to 255, so RGB-to-component translation can look dull or too bright; S-video (Y/C) is better than composite; chroma keys: even lighting, no spill, keep subject away from screen, 4:2:2 or better, detail off; deinterlacing by line doubling, field blending or smart methods; progressive to interlace is trivial (PsF).
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Timecode: hours:minutes:seconds:frames, 24-hour clock; frame counter to :29 (SMPTE), :24 (EBU PAL), :23 (24p); nondrop at 29.97 runs 3.6 seconds long per hour, so drop frame (semicolons) skips two numbers a minute without dropping frames; avoid drop frame at 24p because it complicates pulldown removal; record run, free run and time of day modes; repeating timecode on a tape (DV resets on ejection) is a nightmare, use regen; U-bits carry roll number; jam sync and genlock (tri-level sync) for multicamera.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Monitoring: computer monitors are RGB and show component video flat and dark unless remapped; judge TV work on a Rec. 709 reference or calibrated monitor with blue-only bars; display types (CRT direct light, LCD weak blacks and viewing angle, plasma burn-in, OLED perfect blacks, DLP in cinemas); native resolution, 120/240 Hz motion interpolation changes the look; ambient light affects black; never stretch 4:3 to 16:9; prefer digital connections (HDMI, SDI) over composite.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Pixel aspect ratio: HD and computer pixels are square; SD NTSC 0.9 (widescreen 1.2), PAL 1.066 (widescreen 1.42), 1080 HDV and DVCPRO HD 1.33; titles and stills can distort if not converted. Resolution measures: TV lines per picture height, MTF charts (contrast across line pairs); sharpness depends on contrast, viewing distance and screen size; DPI/PPI is irrelevant to video, only pixel dimensions matter when zooming into stills.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Digital workflow plumbing: USB 2.0 480 Mbps too slow for editing, FireWire 400/800, Thunderbolt 10 Gbps, HDMI (to RGB 4:4:4), SDI 270 Mbps and HD-SDI 1.485 Gbps; RAID 0 striping, 1 mirror, 5 striping with parity (four 1 TB gives 3 TB); a '1 TB' drive holds about 930 GB and should be left 10 to 25 per cent empty; keep media off the system drive; sneakernet is the cheap network. Containers (QuickTime .mov, MP4, MXF, AAF/OMF, XML, DPX) hold media plus metadata; you need the codec as well as the container.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): CBR against VBR (DV 36 Mbps constant; ProRes variable); two-pass VBR for DVDs; JPEG 2000 wavelet for digital cinema; CineForm as intermediate codec; H.265 (HEVC) halves data again.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Footnotes: drop frame skips frame numbers :00 and :01 every minute except each tenth minute (00:04:59:29 is followed by 00:05:00:02); analog NTSC black was raised to 7.5 IRE setup and must be removed when digitising; CRT gamma 2.2 with camera correction 0.45; 18 per cent grey looks halfway between black and white because vision is logarithmic; zebra default on many cameras is nearer 70 per cent; a single 4K Bayer sensor yields about 80 per cent of 4K after demosaicking; CCDs read out row by row while CMOS pixels digitise on-chip.
- **extended** (ch-019.txt): Offline/online today: offline means draft-quality shaping, online means finishing; EDL lists timecode of every shot; proxies (ProRes Proxy, DNxHD 36 at 36 Mbps) relink to full-resolution originals; native editing against transcoding to ProRes, DNxHD or CineForm; compressed 8-bit 4:2:0 hurts titles, keys and recompression, so finish in 4:2:2 10-bit; storage example DV minute 217 MB against more than 17 GB for uncompressed 2K (eighty times); render to an intermediate codec; a clip is a pointer to media, so editing is non-destructive; media off the system drive; pick a codec that does not inflate size needlessly.
- **extended** (ch-019.txt): Mixing formats: frame size, pixel shape, aspect ratio, frame rate and field order all need handling; field order is lower-field-first for NTSC-derived and DV formats and upper-field-first for 1080i HD, PAL SD and computer graphics; downconversion beats upconversion; avoid line doubling and line skipping; use dither when reducing bit depth; prepare stills at twice the project size for a 200 per cent move, about 4,000 px wide for 720p tight zoom; broadcast-safe colours for graphics; vector titles scale cleanly.
- **extended** (ch-020.txt): Delivery of the hybrid finish: conform offline to online by relinking or batch capture, EDL carries In/Out points and reel numbers only, AAF/OMF/XML move more metadata; masters from long-GOP sources should go out in a lighter codec (ProRes 422 or HQ) so later recompression holds up; image sequences (DPX, TIFF) for 2K/4K; web export H.264 plus AAC in MP4, deinterlace, square pixels (720x480 shows as 640x480), start program at 1:00:00:00 after bars, tone, slate and countdown, textless version, test the encode; 44.1 kHz audio on the web.
- **extended** (ch-020.txt): Grading and legality: luma must stay at or below 100 per cent (code 16-235 in 8-bit), chroma below 110 per cent; scopes (waveform, vectorscope with flesh-tone line, RGB parade); primary correction black, white, midtones then colour, secondary correction isolates a colour; LUTs map one master to film-out, DCP or HD; DCP specs: JPEG 2000, 12-bit XYZ, MXF, 24-bit PCM at 48 or 96 kHz, true integer frame rates; master tape leader: 58:30 start, bars and tone, slate, countdown, program at 1:00:00:00; EDL fields (edit number, reel, mode, type, duration, source and record in/out) and A/B/C-mode assembly.
- **extended** (ch-023.txt): Syncing choices in film transfer: in the telecine with timecode (scanners cannot), in a cheaper layback suite, or in the NLE with subframe accuracy; DPX files from scanners go to disk arrays or DLT tape; D.I. term widened to any high-resolution finish; 24 fps NLE timebase gives one-to-one film-frame correspondence; digital dailies in ProRes Proxy or DNxHD help judge sharpness; a 2K/4K scan is a universal master but costly to store, so many scan only the selected shots; transfer to SD is counterproductive.
- **extended** (ch-023.txt): Film data tracking: key numbers permanent and unbroken per camera roll, keycode barcode, in-camera timecode (AatonCode, ARRI Code), audio timecode, telecine video timecode, ink edge code; shot log formats (FLEx, ALE, ATN, FTL) and what to ask for; booking: punch the head of each roll at a key number ending 00, A-frame transfer at an even hour, nondrop timecode, burn-ins, framing chart; transfer takes 1.5-2x running time for one-light dailies, 3-6x with sound and colour, 15-20x for careful grading; transfer sources ranked: original negative, master positive (interpositive), dupe negative, print; one universal 1080p/24 master for deliverables.
- **extended** (ch-023.txt): Matchback: A-frame pulldown phases (A1 A2, B1-B3, C1 C2, D1-D3; A frames have timecode ending :00 or :05), pull-in; keycode is the most reliable reference across transfers; confidence list check; matchback from a 30 fps offline can add or drop a frame (at most plus or minus one), so leave two video frames as cutting frames; dupe list, pull list, assemble list, optical list, change list; fades and dissolves in standard lab lengths of 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96 frames; film-out via laser recorder (Arrilaser), kinescope; 25p film-out runs 4 per cent slow; crop 2 per cent for 1.85; reels of about 20 minutes.
- **note** (ch-019.txt): NLE mechanics (insert/overwrite, extract/lift, three-point editing, ripple/roll/slip/slide trims, handles of half the dissolve length, L- and J-cuts, crossfades, sync breaks, speed effects with frame blending and optical flow, upscaling 25 per cent in HD, stabilisation): useful to the capstone workflow but beyond the course's scope; no change.

### cinematography-6

- **confirmed** (ch-005.txt): Super 8 introduced by Kodak in 1965 with a frame 50 per cent larger than regular 8mm in an easy cartridge; regular 8mm arrived 1932 (half the width of 16mm image, twice the perfs); 16mm came in the 1920s as an amateur format and its frame is a quarter of the 35mm area.
- **confirmed** (ch-006.txt): Film shot at 24 fps for 25 fps television is sped up by 4 per cent; 24p to PAL 25 changes speed and pitch.
- **confirmed** (ch-012.txt): Tungsten stock 500T rated 320 in daylight with an 85 (about two-thirds of a stop); 80A on daylight stock costs two stops; faster stocks have larger crystals and more grain; ISO doubling is one stop; DIN marking (500/28 degrees); T and D suffix for tungsten and daylight; film IDs such as 5279 where 52 means 35mm and 72 means 16mm.
- **confirmed** (ch-011.txt): (carried from the earlier review) 16 mm 400 ft runs about 11 minutes; storage temperatures; filter factors 85 at 1.6 and 80A at 4.
- **refined** (ch-011.txt): (carried from the earlier review) The viewfinder does not show the exposed frame: mirror shutters go dark while exposing and beam splitters cost a third to a full stop. Also: gate check, scratch, light leak and framing tests; eyepiece light trap; X-ray accumulation.
- **contradicted** (ch-023.txt): Again the handbook says 35mm runs at 96 feet a minute (2,000-foot reels of 20-21 minutes, 1,900 ft of picture); 4-perf 35mm has 16 frames to the foot, so 24 fps is 90 ft a minute and 1,000 ft is 11.1 minutes. Course keeps 90 ft/min and flags the book's figure; trust arithmetic from 16 frames per foot over the book's 96 figure.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Super 16 has one row of perfs and a frame 40 per cent larger than 16mm at 1.67:1, nearly 16:9 so HD transfer needs negligible cropping; Super 35 reclaims the sound-track area for a 32 per cent larger image and must be scanned; three-perf saves 25 per cent of stock; two-perf Techniscope saves 50 per cent at 2.40:1; 65mm shot, 70mm shown; IMAX runs film horizontally at fifteen perfs.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Nitrate base was flammable and replaced in the early 1950s by acetate safety film, now often polyester. Intermittent movement: claw pulls film while shutter blocks light. Reversal film shows a positive straight from processing; negative must be printed. Magnification to a modest screen is about 100,000 times for 16mm and over 300,000 times for Super 8.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Film versus digital: film costs more per minute but a film rig may rent for much less per day than a high-end digital camera; film stocks hold a wide tonal range; film is simpler in heat and power; it forces planning and a low shooting ratio; archival digital playback is uncertain while film keeps if stored well. Labs were closing.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Characteristic curve: D-min (base plus fog), threshold, toe, straight line, shoulder, D-max; expose important tones on the straight line; shadows near threshold go to featureless black, highlights high on the shoulder compress; gamma is the slope of the straight line (colour negative about 0.55). Halation is light scattering in the base back into the emulsion, curbed by antihalation backing; three dye layers (yellow, magenta, cyan) with orange mask on negatives.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Push and pull: pushing rates film higher and extends development (double ISO per stop pushed) which raises contrast and grain but not shadow detail; pulling overexposes and underdevelops to cut contrast and grain; flashing lifts shadows (milky, grainier); bleach bypass leaves silver for high contrast and desaturation, test first; negative has more latitude than reversal; reversal pushed goes muddy.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Choosing a stock: slowest film that gives the f-stop wanted; order tungsten-balanced stock for flexibility because the 85 costs only two-thirds of a stop outdoors, while 80A costs four times the light indoors; low-contrast stocks suit direct transfer to digital; overexposing colour negative slightly reduces grain but overexposing black and white increases it; keep the full emulsion number as a check; Kodak Look Manager previews stocks.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Film handling: use raw stock within six months; below 55 F (13 C) for under three months, freezer 0 to -10 F for longer; warm to room temperature before opening the seal; X-ray is cumulative, never check unprocessed film, hand-carry and ask for a hand inspection, label 'No X-ray'; test 20 ft for fog; key numbers every half foot in 16mm (20 frames) and every foot in 35mm (16 frames), zero-frame dot; keycode barcode; A-wind and B-wind; single-perf needed for Super 16.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Metering: incident meters read light falling on the subject (hemisphere dome points at camera) and suit faces; reflected meters read luminance and aim to render any surface as middle grey, so a black cat reads too bright and must be given less exposure; 18 per cent grey card; average Caucasian skin about 35 per cent reflectance, open one stop from a skin reading; spot meters have a narrow angle (about 1 degree); use T-stops for exposure calculations; beam-splitter viewfinders need an effective shutter speed (Bolex 1/65 actual, 1/80 effective at 24 fps); precision beyond a third of a stop is pointless; contrasty scenes need interpretation or added fill.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Exposure strategy: base on what matters (face), faces: open one stop for pale skin and close half to one stop for dark skin from a reflected reading; average bright and dark readings in stops not arithmetic (f/2 and f/16 average f/5.6); backlight rule open 1.5 stops above the reflected reading to avoid silhouette, close back half a stop if flare is severe; haze adds exposure; sunrise bracket half to one stop each way; night scenes need bright highlights to read dark.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Latitude: colour negative about ten to twelve stops total range, reversal about six; negative tolerates 1-1.5 stops under and 2 or more over, reversal about a stop; the word means both total range and tolerated error; higher lighting contrast leaves less leeway; slight overexposure reduces grain and enriches blacks, underexposure gives grain and smoky blacks; overexposure raises telecine gain noise; printing down will not restore highlights.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Lab practice: tag cans EXPOSED with title, stock, emulsion number, footage, special processing, camera roll number (never repeat); keep the title unchanged; lab report notes scratches, dirt, flicker; one-light, best-light and timed workprint; troubleshooting: cinch marks, white sparkle dirt on negative, edge fog from light leaks, gate hairs, stock defects; scratch on emulsion versus base and diagnosis by reflection.
- **extended** (ch-023.txt): Traditional finishing: A-roll single strand versus A&B rolls (checkerboard) hide 16mm splices over black leader and allow fades, dissolves and supers; printer lights in 50 steps, normal near 25-30, one stop of overexposure needs about +6 or +7 points; additive printing; answer print then release prints; intermediates (master positive gamma 1.0, dupe negative, internegative, YCM separations) after about ten prints; optical sound sits 26 frames ahead in 16mm and 20 in 35mm, so pullups are needed when reels are spliced; Super 16 designed for 35mm blowup, slightly overexpose up to a stop for finer grain; changeover marks on frames 25-28 and 196-199.

### cinematography-5

- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): Jump cuts avoided by changing shot size and moving laterally, with a guide of at least 30 degrees; script supervisor; cutaways cover discontinuity (speech edit); overlap action across shots (car door example); single-camera drama builds continuous time from takes shot on different days.
- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): 180-degree rule: draw the line of action (eye line in conversation, car movement, football field), keep cameras one side so screen direction holds, neutral shots on the line bridge sides, crossing during a take is acceptable, chases and shot/reverse-shot depend on it; in a car scene draw the line along the couple's eye line not the road.
- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): Scheduling: low-budget day is about three or four script pages in twelve hours; script breakdown in eighths of a page, stripboard colour-coded interior/exterior day/night; group scenes by location and actor (day out of days); easier scenes first, no key scene on day one, exteriors early with interior cover set, duplicate wardrobe; meal break every six hours; turnaround at least twelve hours; plan reshoots and pickups. Shooting ratio: drama about 5:1 to 15:1, reality TV up to 450 hours per hour; film imposes discipline, digital loosens it; 'pre-editing' coverage cuts footage; Hitchcock's precision (Tomasini quip) as an extreme.
- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): Slider moves: even a two-foot slider with a wide lens and a slow glide of six seconds or more adds value, movement reads best past foreground objects; sliders suit DSLR weight.
- **contradicted** (ch-014.txt): (carried from the earlier review) 'Start with the hardest scene' was our rule; the handbook suggests easier scenes first, exteriors early, no key scene on day one. Both views are shown.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Vocabulary: scene, sequence, setup (new camera position or lighting, not a mere lens change), take, shot; shot sizes long, medium, close-up, big close-up, extreme close-up, two-button close-up, dirty close-up, shot/reverse shot, two-shot, point-of-view; composition guides: rule of thirds (eyes a third from top) that many good frames ignore, leading the action (leave room in the direction of movement or look), headroom is subjective, Dutch angle, shoot objects at an angle for depth, give scale references; Hollywood deep space against flat European 1960s-70s frames.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Frame safety: TV cutoff/overscan crops CRT edges, safe action and safe title areas, underscan on monitors, shoot a framing chart when cropping 16:9 to 1.85 or 2.35 in post. Camera moves: pans motivated by subject, landscape pans slow to avoid judder, swish pan avoids strobing, larger screens exaggerate moves; dolly changes perspective while zoom magnifies and flattens; treadmill effect from zooming against movement; Vertigo, Jaws and GoodFellas dolly against zoom; bury a zoom in a pan; motorised zoom for smoothness.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Style: mise-en-scène (long take, deep focus, Bazin, Keaton) against montage; classic Hollywood master-shot coverage then four-angle two-person scene (master, two-shot, close-up, reverse); Cassavetes, music-video cutting; MOS from German 'mit-out-sprache' story; coverage means angles beyond the master, and editors lament too little; Allen's uninterrupted masters against Touch of Evil's three-and-a-half minute opening crane shot; long to medium to close-up delves into a scene, widening signals a larger event or leave-taking.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Point of view: same doctor sequence shot three ways (with the man, with his wife, with the doctor first so the audience knows more than the man); Hitchcock's bomb under the table, fifteen seconds of surprise against fifteen minutes of suspense (quote from Truffaut interviews); eye line near the lens gives subjective feel (Rashomon, Last Picture Show), looking into the lens is awkward; wobbly handheld equals interiority by convention; Rear Window look-POV-reaction push-in; Psycho prowling camera; reveal by blocking, mystery.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Time: compress with dissolve, reveal (close-up pulls back to finished painting), cutaway; walking out of frame permits a time jump; expand with blocking, slow motion, Raging Bull's mix of speeds; jump cuts now common. Documentary: verité/direct cinema, Grierson, personal documentary, B-roll, Wiseman real-time scenes; shoot movements with static head and tail holds; cover long scenes with varied angles, listening shots, over-the-shoulder, neutral shots with no visible lips or fingers; interviews: ask for full-sentence answers, no references to earlier talk.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Preparation: table reads, rehearsal (Mike Leigh), floor plans, storyboards, video previs (Coppola), shooting script with locked scene numbers and coloured revision pages (blue then pink then yellow); one page a minute rule; Hitchcock previsualised so fully that shooting was execution; interviews: ask for re-asks at a different focal length, multi-camera avoids fake reaction shots (Broadcast News), Morris's Interrotron, alternate screen direction, leave room for lower-thirds; crew roles list (1st AD, script supervisor, DP, 1st AC, clapper loader, DIT, gaffer, grips, sound recordist).
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Pre-production and set: location technical survey (direction, lighting and sun path, power, sound, parking and permits), director's viewfinder, begin preproduction three to four months ahead; slate protocol (sound speed, camera speed, mark, head slate versus tail slate held upside down, second sticks), scene and take numbering (8, 8A), shoot the slate large and in focus, slate MOS takes; record room tone and wild lines; cover reactions, cutaways and insurance shots; Lumet few takes against Kubrick many, at least two keepers; field equipment package checklist; crew size trade-offs; casting breakdown and sides; pickups with stills for matching.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Supports: fluid heads best, friction cheap, geared repeatable; balance and lock the head; level the tripod to avoid canted pans; spreader, quick-release plate, hi-hat, dual-stage legs, apple boxes; door dolly, crab dolly, boom, jib, track levelled with wedges; dolly grip is an extension of the operator. Vehicles: bigger car smoother, low tyre pressure, shooting at right angles makes a car look about twice as fast, wide lenses increase apparent speed, picture car towed for actors' safety. Handheld: shoulder-mounted steadiest, rigs and cages, Groucho walk, count to six without moving, movement memory aid.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Working with actors: only the director gives performance notes, clear the set for intimate scenes, stand-ins for lighting, spike marks, do not hide in video village, give the director a feed of recorded sound; Huston: the art of direction is casting. Wardrobe: avoid pure white and fine checks (moiré), dulling spray, powder for shine, light glasses from high or side. Logging: log fields (card, scene, take, timecode, good), continuity script with lined script, camera and sound reports with circled takes.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Editing theory: Kuleshov experiments (same neutral face with soup, injured girl, gun; order changes meaning), Eisenstein's film space and time as montage constructs (Potemkin baby carriage, October peacock), Hollywood adopted the three-shot look-cut-reaction pattern (Rear Window); cut on action; match cuts versus jump cuts (Godard's Breathless); straight cuts between sequences, dissolve and fade grammar; screen direction at cuts, neutral shot repairs 180 violations, travel left to right reads west to east; intercutting (Out of Sight) and freeze frames; Murch quoting Fleming: great editing makes a film look undirected.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Dialogue editing: condense speech with cutaways and listening shots, split edits or L-cuts (sound before or after picture), cutting away before a question ends feels less mechanical; Hitchcock held that what is said should contrast with what is seen; ADR/looping with beeps and streamers; chopped-off words fixed with a two-frame crossfade; rough cut long then fine cut, picture lock, change lists; check on a big screen and with fresh viewers; Murch warns instant NLE access loses serendipity; avoid over-preselecting from transcripts.
- **note** (ch-006.txt): Chapter 2 opens with planning and funding (logline, core audience, working backward from distribution and budget, cut scenes and locations to fit money, do not fund on credit cards). Useful for the capstone planning habit: decide the end screen and delivery spec before choosing the format. Theatrical projection standard is 24 fps and 16:9 or wider; digital cinema package (DCP) is the encrypted standard set of files.
- **note** (ch-014.txt): 3D: interaxial about 65 mm (2.5 in), convergence, vergence/accommodation conflict is the cause of eyestrain, positive and negative parallax, long lenses flatten (View-Master effect), side-by-side versus mirror rigs, The Amazing Spider-Man used 0.25-0.75 in interaxial; RealD 144 flashes a second (3 per frame at 24 fps). Out of scope for the course; no change.
- **note** (ch-018.txt): Length and titles: features about 90-120 minutes, TV hour about 57 or 52 minutes, education short, corporate 10-15 minutes; titles in TV safe title area, drop shadows, no thin serifs, line height not below 1/25 of image height, 40 characters per line, credit roll 7-12 seconds bottom to top, keep read-twice rule, leave room at frame bottom for lower thirds, keep textless version. Capstone planning could add a delivery-length check; no course change needed.
- **note** (ch-022.txt): Sound editing and mixing (spotting, track splitting, checkerboarding, room tone, walla, temp music, Foley, OMF/AAF, reel leaders with sync pop, compressors and limiters, loudness -24 LKFS +/-2 in the US and -23 LUFS in Europe) is outside the cinematography course; sound's importance to audiences matches ch 11 and ch 6. Useful cross-reference for the directing course on Hitchcock's sound.
- **note** (ch-024.txt): Chapter 17 (funding, budgets with 5-15 per cent contingency, crew rates, insurance, copyright, releases, music clearance with sync and master-use licences, fair use four factors, distribution windows, festivals, marketing) is outside the cinematography course. Relevant caution for the capstone: clear music, locations and appearances before showing work publicly.

### cinematography-3

- **refined** (ch-006.txt): Course credits Toland's deep focus in Citizen Kane to small apertures; the handbook credits wide-angle lenses, bright lights and faster film stocks together to overcome the shallow depth of field of typical 35mm. Small aperture needs the extra light. Course wording should name all three.
- **contradicted** (ch-008.txt): (carried from the earlier review) A course caption said each stop doubles depth of field; a doubling of the f-number (two stops) doubles it. Corrected, our own error. Also the handbook's 25 mm f/2 at 4 ft example gives 7 inches against about 9.6 by the standard formulas; the handbook figure was not used.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Large-screen projection magnifies shake and focus errors; 35mm look includes grain, unsteady projection and judder artefacts such as backward-spinning wagon wheels, which are not by definition good; Cassavetes' handheld 16mm shows a smaller gauge can suit the work.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Sharpness depends less on fine detail than on bold black-to-white contrast, so contrast changes can make a low-resolution image look sharper; edge-enhancement (detail) circuits add thin halos and a videolike look; diffusion filters and smoke deliberately throw away resolution; the image cannot be better than the lens, so test any lens including stills lenses on DSLRs.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Anamorphic lens: classic squeeze factor 2 doubles horizontal angle of view only, so matching a spherical angle needs twice the focal length, giving proportionally shallower depth of field, larger heavier slower glass and more light; Hawk 1.3 squeeze suits 16:9 sensors; a large sensor does not guarantee shallow depth in every shot; cine adapters for small sensors cost several stops.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Aspect conversion: letterbox, pillarbox, edge crop, pan and scan, squeeze; 4:3 into 16:9 by enlarging loses 25 per cent of resolution; postage stamp (windowbox) to avoid; protect 14:9 and keep graphics in 4:3 safe area; 4:3 suits a face while 16:9 shows more background; windowing on taller DSLR sensors; three-perf and two-perf routes to 16:9 and 2.39.
- **extended** (ch-026.txt): Circle of confusion by format: 0.025 mm for 35mm film, 0.015 mm for 16mm, DSLR 0.030 mm full frame, 0.020 mm Super 35, 0.019 mm APS-C, 0.015 mm Four Thirds (so 16mm film and Four Thirds share a value); depth-of-field tables are approximations; T-stop tables with f-stop geometry give a slightly stingy figure; hyperfocal focus gives acceptable focus from half the hyperfocal distance to infinity. 100 mm at T8 focused at 10 ft gives 9 ft to 11 ft 4 in.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt): (carried from the earlier review) Normal lens angles (about 40 degrees stills, 24 degrees Academy); parfocal against varifocal zooms; split focus; hyperfocal distance; flare; diffraction by sensor size; aspect ratios 1.85 and 1.66; chart accuracy 15-20 per cent.

### cinematography-4

- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): Presets 3200 K tungsten and 5600 K daylight; a 5600 K filter wheel (like an 85) costs about two-thirds of a stop; manual white balance on a white or grey card in the same light as the subject, exposure set first; professional cameras store two balances.
- **refined** (ch-017.txt): (carried from the earlier review) Colour temperature table now shows both the handbook (household bulbs about 2,900 K, sunrise 2,000 K, overcast 6,000-7,500 K) and the other source. 'Fill up to half the key' was clarified: key-to-fill 2:1 is lighting contrast (K+F):F of 3:1.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): In black and white a green leaf and a red apple may render as one grey, so lighting needs strong backlight or rim light to separate subjects; there is no need to match the colour of sources; most modern monochrome is shot in colour and desaturated.
- **extended** (ch-017.txt): (carried from the earlier review) Mired shifts, conversion filter costs, mixed light, key placement about 45 degrees, soft light fall-off, practicals two to three stops above faces, dimmers lower colour temperature, safety, power budget, incident metering for contrast.

Totals: 27 confirmed, 8 refined, 4 contradicted, 83 extended, 0 absent, 7 note.
